summary: This deck contrasts corporate and grassroots frugal innovation, explaining how firms and communities create affordable solutions under resource constraints through top-down and bottom-up approaches. It uses case studies including Mettler Toledo, Accor Ibis Budget, Local Motors, Fairwaves, Braigo, BrickPi, and Foldscope to show cost reduction, standardization, open innovation, and local problem-solving. The deck also discusses cannibalization, the limits of each approach, polycentric innovation, and the role of frugal innovation in inclusive development, poverty reduction, and social impact.

content: Companies realized that billions of low-income people can also be customers. Selling affordable products to this large market can become a profitable business.
Companies can do two things together
Help poor people access useful products
Example: A low-cost medical diagnostic device can improve healthcare while generating revenue.
Companies first choose a target customer group and then design products specifically for their needs.
After understanding customers, companies remove features that are not necessary and reduces cost.
The main reason companies pursue frugal innovation is business growth. Companies earn less profit on each product.
Corporate frugal innovation is the art of delivering only what customers truly need, at the lowest possible cost, without compromising quality.
Corporate Frugal Innovation: Deliver affordable, high-quality, profitable products through systematic engineering and large-scale production.
Corporate and Grassroot Frugal Innovation: A Comparison of Top-Down and Bottom-Up Strategies

Mettler Toledo followed a structured process-

Case study 2: Accor Ibis Budget hotel chain
There were many traveling salespeople who
Needed a clean and comfortable place to sleep.
Traditional hotels were too expensive, while very cheap hotels often had poor quality.
Focus on essential customer needs and eliminate non-essential features.
Suppose a customer normally stays in an expensive Accor hotel.
The customer shifts to Ibis Budget (low-cost hotel brand owned by Accor).
Accor loses revenue from its premium hotel.
Customer → Leaves Accor → Goes to a competitor.
Customer → Stays within Accor's hotel portfolio.
So although Accor earns less money from that customer, it still retains the customer.
Ibis Budget case demonstrates that successful corporate frugal innovation is about:
Using standardization and automation to reduce costs.
Maintaining acceptable quality and brand reputation.

Local Motors is an American automotive company that introduced a microfactory model for designing and manufacturing vehicles. Instead of relying on large, centralized factories, it uses small, local production facilities supported by open innovation and crowdsourcing.
Open-source design: Vehicle designs are created and improved by a global online community of engineers, designers, and enthusiasts.
Crowd-powered innovation: Ideas and designs come from thousands of contributors rather than only an in-house R&D team.
Microfactory concept: Small manufacturing units located close to customers reduce transportation costs and enable localized production.
Maker spaces: Microfactories also function as innovation hubs where students, inventors, and local communities can collaborate.
High-performance sports car with high degree of flexibility.
Reduced development time from about 60 months to 18 months.
Reduced development cost from around US$1 billion to about US$3 million.
Case Study 4: Fairwaves – Low-Cost GSM Base Station
Fairwaves is a startup originating from Neuron Hackspace (Moscow) that develops low-cost GSM base stations for affordable mobile communication, particularly in low-income and rural regions.
Base station cost: ~US$5,000 (compared to millions for conventional telecom infrastructure).
Built using the open-source Osmocom GSM software stack.
Managed remotely using a standard laptop.
Open-source software reduces development and licensing costs.
Energy-efficient design with minimal power requirements.
Scalable architecture from a single base station to nationwide deployment.
Affordable connectivity, enabling mobile services for about US$1–2 per month.

Fairwaves demonstrates how frugal engineering can dramatically reduce the cost and complexity of mobile communication infrastructure, making telecommunications accessible in resource-constrained regions.

Briago braille printer (braigolabs.com): Young inventor Shubham Banerjee used the Lego Mindstorms EV3 kit($349) and a few parts from a hardware store to create a Braille printer that costs just $350 (compared to$2000 for a conventional machine).

BrickPi Bookreader: Invented by John Cole, BrickPi scans the pages of physical books. His digitizer uses the $30 Raspberry Pi computer, and overall costs $450 compared to $16000 for conventional equipment.
Foldscope (foldscope.com). Foldscope is a 2,000X magnification optical microscope that can be printed, cut, and assembled from a flat sheet of paper for less than $1.

In each of the cases, the goals are environmental, social, or economic to various degrees, but each case has used ingenious ways to address the challenges of limited resources and turn them into an advantage.

Grassroots Frugal Innovations (GFIs) are low-cost solutions developed by ordinary people or local communities to solve everyday problems using locally available resources. They are the oldest form of frugal innovation and originated mainly in India and China.
GFIs are the foundation of frugal engineering.

Although GFIs often lack formal education, advanced technology, funding, and engineering support, they are able to develop innovative products through creativity, practical experience, problem-solving ability, hard work.
Grassroots innovators can achieve much more if they receive better education, access to scientific and engineering knowledge, financial assistance, technical guidance, affordable research facilities

Differences between corporate versus grassroot frugal innovation
Driver | Companies | Individual inventors who are part of or close to the target group
Impulse | Market opportunity | Clever idea to solve a problem
Target | High profitability targeted | Low economic profitability accepted
Quality | In line with brand | Good enough for target customers
Production Scale | Mass manufacturing | Single items and small series
Development Process | Complex, resource-intensive | Simple, resource-restricted
| Elaborate prototypes | Early, fast, frequent prototyping
Success Factors | Dedicated corporate R&D teams, close collaboration with customers | Input from other designers, collaborative/crowd design
Challenges | Cannibalization of existing offerings; brand damage | Upscaling

Can frugal innovation contribute to economic development, poverty reduction, and inclusive growth, especially in developing countries?
Frugal innovation should not be viewed only as low-cost product development. It is a much broader concept involving technology, business models, institutions, entrepreneurship, and social inclusion.
Frugal innovation is viewed from a business perspective. Companies develop products that are Affordable, Good quality, Resource efficient for emerging markets.
Frugal emphasize poverty reduction, employment, access to healthcare, access to energy, education
Frugal Innovation as a Combination of Top-down and Bottom-up Innovation
Top-down innovation is driven by large corporations adapting products for new markets, whereas bottom-up innovation originates from grassroots communities solving immediate local problems
Frugal Innovation is More Than Cheap Products
Frugal innovation should include new business models, new delivery systems, institutional innovation, social innovation, entrepreneurship, local capability building
